A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching renamed attacks and relocated analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original forgery, removal and reprompting experiments, together with transferability, perturbation and finetuning analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds baseline comparisons and sampler/inversion-step ablations in Appendices C and E.

M1.justification: The proposed latent optimization losses, masking extension, removal procedure, reprompting and bin resampling remain unchanged. Imprinting is renamed Imprint-Forgery, and the existing removal variant receives its own subsection.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix C introduces ImageNet validation images and watermarked images prompted with ImageNet class names for training the Surrogate baseline. The original prompt datasets, COCO cover images, anime data and principal forgery/removal tasks remain.

E2.justification: v1 has no evaluated forgery baseline and compares removal only with AdvEmb. v2 evaluates Averaging for forgery and adds Averaging, Regeneration and Surrogate to the removal comparison. AdvEmb is retained in Appendix C, Table 5, although Averaging replaces it in the main removal table.

E3.justification: Appendices C and E introduce averaging protocols using 10–5,000 reference images, surrogate-classifier training, regeneration settings, and DDIM/DPM and 10–100 inversion-step comparisons over 30 attack samples. The retained encoder-similarity analysis changes its reported metric from cosine to absolute cosine similarity, although its numerical heatmap is unchanged. Main attack budgets and detection thresholds remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled analyses of attacker/defender sampler choices and attacker inversion steps, testing attack effectiveness and image-quality tradeoffs. It also analyzes reference-image counts for Averaging and expands qualitative baseline comparisons. The earlier transferability, common-perturbation and finetuning analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: New Tables 4–5 tabulate ± variability for bit accuracy and p-values, alongside additional PSNR spread figures; their precise statistical interpretation is not defined. Appendix C specifies 30 randomly drawn reference subsets for Averaging. v1 already displayed result distributions, and v2 does not establish increased repeated runs of the original attacks.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline results and sampler-ablation findings. Existing Table 1 values also change: FLUX.1 Tree-Ring forgery detection at 150 steps changes from 0.28 to 0.23, and Gaussian Shading detection/attribution at 100 steps from 0.88 to 0.86. Several PSNR and AdvEmb values change, while Table 3's reprompting results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v1 Section 4.3 explicitly defines AdvEmb through a constrained maximization objective; v2 omits that mathematical specification while retaining the baseline's settings in Appendix C. The diffusion equations, proposed attack losses and Gaussian Shading false-positive formula remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims retain the same scope: single-reference forgery/removal using unrelated models and ineffective threshold defenses. Added comparison evidence and the conclusion's security-auditing recommendation do not redefine these central scientific claims.

C2.justification: v2 expands the existing unique-key argument into a discussion of deployment ambiguity, key management and alleged key/nonce reuse in earlier evaluations. It adds sampler-defense interpretations and qualifies v1's universal claim about pixel relocation destroying watermarks. Some new wording overreaches: Appendix C says only the proposed attacks remove Gaussian Shading, although Table 5 reports partial Regeneration success on FLUX.1, with detection remaining at 0.64.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code link and detailed baseline implementation repositories, training settings, perturbation budgets and reference-sampling instructions. It specifies Tree-Ring insertion into the third latent channel, identifies FLUX.1's scheduler as FlowMatchEuler, and explains finetuning-threshold calibration. Fresh per-image keys/nonces clarify the retained setup rather than establish a procedural change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops its positioning against prior attacks, including an explanation of conflicting Gaussian Shading findings through key/nonce reuse. It adds Thietke et al.'s cryptographic-usage study and two post-hoc forgery references, while removing AquaLoRA and ControlNet citations. The retitled averaging paper and updated WAVES reference represent retained works.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes attack names, separates removal into Section 3.2, edits passages and captions, and adds an appendix contents page. New appendix sections shift existing sections' lettering, but most of the original narrative and overall organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds full comparison Tables 4–5 and the multi-panel sampler ablation in Figure 19, and expands main Tables 1–2 with baseline rows. The narrow AdvEmb visual comparison becomes a larger forgery/removal comparison. Existing quality-tradeoff plots are relocated, while robustness and finetuning figures receive clearer panel labels and revised captions.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked an evaluated forgery baseline and compared removal only with AdvEmb. v2's broader comparisons make relative effectiveness and reference-image requirements substantially more assessable, while sampler ablations and deployment clarification address practical assumptions behind the attacks. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including overbroad baseline-failure wording and inconsistent FLUX.1 Gaussian Shading removal PSNR at 50 steps: 30.11 in Table 2 versus 30.31 in Table 5.
